questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A district ordered to plant for the market

options.misconception: ignores the compulsory element of the scheme

options.text: It freed the district from subsistence farming, because the villagers were paid in cash for the crop
options.misconception: assumes cash payment replaced subsistence

options.text: It concentrated the crop in one district only, leaving all other districts free to plant as they wished
options.misconception: invents a concentration policy the order lacks

options.text: It tied the household's subsistence to a market quota set far away, so local food use became secondary

questions.explanation: The order set a quota households had to meet, so land was tied to a distant market, not to local needs. The alternatives treat it as a bonus, a cash windfall or a localised experiment.
questions.hint: Ask what the household had to do first.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A debt that could not be walked away from
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an advance of money became inescapable bondage
questions.stem: Explain how a labour system that began with an advance of money became a form of bondage that could not be walked away from.

answer.exemplar: A man who travelled to a plantation far from his village needed money for the journey, so a recruiter advanced it and recorded the sum against his name with a term of years attached. On arrival he was housed, fed and clothed on credit, and each month of wages was credited first against the debt of the journey and the cost of what he had consumed, so that a worker who was ill, idle or badly paid could not reduce what he owed. The contract looked like employment, but because the debt grew with the very needs it was supposed to meet, and because leaving meant owing more, the labourer stayed longer than any term he had agreed to.

questions.explanation: The debt was measured in money but grew with the worker's needs, so leaving increased it and the term could not be completed. The account that the worker simply served an agreed term ignores how the debt rolled on.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the balance when a worker fell ill.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A bounded term of service and what it changed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a limit on campaigns was introduced in a republic
questions.stem: Explain why a limit on the number of campaigns a soldier might serve was introduced in a republic, and what the limit was intended to achieve.

answer.exemplar: In the republic described by Polybius, a soldier was bound to serve a fixed number of campaigns and no more, and the age at which he might begin and the age at which he must leave were also fixed, so that no man could make a career of arms and accumulate the influence that long service and command brought. The purpose was to keep the army a body of citizens renewed from the population rather than a permanent force of veterans whose loyalty was owed to their generals, and to prevent the experience and following of old soldiers from turning into political weight. The term was thus an institution of the civic order, not merely an administrative arrangement about pay and discharge.

questions.explanation: A bounded term kept the army tied to the citizen body and denied old soldiers the influence that long service brought, so the limit protected the republic's politics. The reading that it was mere administration misses its purpose.
questions.hint: Ask what long service made possible politically.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a settlement after a rebellion organised
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a post-rebellion settlement built and why it failed
questions.stem: Explain what the settlement made at the Restoration organised, and which questions it deliberately left open.

answer.exemplar: The settlement of 1660 settled who would hold the Crown and on what advice, restored the Church of England with the bishops who had been imprisoned, and confirmed the property arrangements of the years before the war, all in the interest of the landed interest that had driven the rising. It then found ways to leave the questions that might have divided the ruling class undecided: the succession was left open, the militia was left in a state that neither the Crown nor Parliament could control, and the new religious settlement was framed so that the sects could be tolerated without being equal. In that sense the Restoration was less a settlement of the country's divisions than a distribution of them.

questions.explanation: The settlement fixed the Crown, the Church and property for those who had caused the war, and left succession, the militia and the sects unresolved, so divisions were managed rather than solved. Saying it settled everything misses the ambiguity.
questions.hint: Ask which questions were put off.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A district ordered to plant for the market
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a company ordered a district to plant its raw material
questions.stem: Explain why a company that needed a raw material for its trade ordered a whole district to plant it, and what that arrangement did to the people who lived there.

answer.exemplar: A company that sold pepper, cloves or cinnamon in Europe had to secure a regular supply at a price it could live with, and the surest way was to control the growing rather than to bargain for it in the market. Where the growing was placed under company supervision, plots were allotted, trees were counted, and the crop was collected and paid for on terms set elsewhere. For the cultivators this meant that their land, their labour and their food were organised around a demand felt far away, and that an official sat in the village recording what had been planted; the arrangement removed the market risk from the trade and placed it on the growers instead.

questions.explanation: Controlling production moved the risk of price and supply from the company to the growers, whose land and labour were tied to a demand they did not set. The account credits the scheme with prosperity rather than obligation.
questions.hint: Ask who carried the risk of a bad price.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how legal freedom could create a labour shortage
questions.stem: Explain how a change in the legal status of a people could create a labour shortage for those who had relied on them, and why the shortage was not always understood as one.

answer.exemplar: When a labouring population becomes legally free, the work it had been compelled to perform no longer follows it to the fields and the workshops of those who had depended on it, and the first season after the change can find employers competing for hands they had never had to bid for. The shortage is often described as a transitional difficulty and is met by raising wages, by recruiting from a distance, or by pressing the law into stricter service, since employers have an interest in finding the cheapest way to hold labour in place. What makes the shortage hard to understand is that the legal change was an improvement in the condition of most of the people concerned, and the hardship fell on those who had benefited from the old system.

questions.explanation: Freedom removed the compulsion that had supplied employers' labour, so the shortage was a real effect of the change even though the change was a gain for the freed. Calling it proof the reform was harmful confuses two interests.
questions.hint: Ask whose benefit the shortage threatened.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how surveyed title replaced tracing possession
questions.stem: Explain how title based on a survey and a public register replaced title based on tracing the occupation of land, and what cost the new system carried.

answer.exemplar: Under the older practice a buyer's title consisted of the chain of conveyances by which the land had passed from one holder to the next, and his safety depended on every one of those documents being good, which meant searching archives, reading deeds and accepting the risk of a flaw in some remote transfer. The surveyed title inverts the process: a single register entry records the parcel, its boundaries and its current holder, and the registrar guarantees it, so a buyer inspects one entry rather than a chain. The cost is that the state's survey and its officers become indispensable, since the entry is only as good as the survey on which it rests, and disputes about a boundary become disputes about the surveyor's work rather than about old possession.

questions.explanation: A single guaranteed register entry replaced the need to search a chain of deeds, shortening conveyancing but making the survey decisive. The account that it removed all risk misses what it transferred to the state.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a trading concession actually conceded
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a trading concession usually conceded
questions.stem: Explain what a trading concession usually conceded, and why the wording of such grants has been read as giving far more than trade.

answer.exemplar: A trading concession typically conveyed a defined right for a defined term: the right to build and work a route or a works, the right to take a toll or a share of the returns, the right to hold the lands needed for it, and often the right to govern the people living on those lands, to keep an armed force and to make the regulations of the passage. Because the grantee was a company rather than a sovereign, these clauses were framed as commercial concessions while in practice conferring the powers of government; the bargain was usually cheap for the state, which received a share of the receipts and a claim on European capital, and expensive for the grantee, which bore the cost of construction and the risk of the traffic.

questions.explanation: The grants were framed as commercial rights but carried governmental powers over land, people and armed force, so a concession was a transfer of authority dressed as a contract. The account that they were merely commercial misreads their clauses.
questions.hint: Ask what the grantee was allowed to do to people.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A reform dated by the crisis that produced it
questions.learningObjective: Explain what is gained by dating a reform by its crisis
questions.stem: Explain why historians date some reforms by the crisis that produced them, and what is gained and lost by such a naming.

answer.exemplar: Naming a measure for the year of the disturbance that forced it does two things. It marks the reform as an answer to an emergency, which is why such laws tend to be narrow, to name the occasion in their own titles, and to lapse when the occasion passes. It also keeps the memory of the crisis attached to the measure, so that a reader judging the reform later is reminded that it was born of a moment rather than of a settled view of society. What is lost is the sequence: the arguments and the failed proposals that preceded the statute are usually dated by the debates rather than by the year of the crisis, and a law's title can therefore hide the longer disagreement in which it was a single move.

questions.explanation: Dating a reform by its crisis marks it as an emergency response and keeps the memory of the disturbance attached, but the title hides the arguments that came before. The claim that the naming is neutral misses both effects.
questions.hint: Ask what the title carries with it.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how an employer's advance became a rolling debt
questions.stem: Explain how a system in which an employer advanced money and food could keep a worker in conditions resembling slavery, and what the law's response was.

answer.exemplar: If an employer advanced money for the journey and then supplied the worker with food and clothing on credit, every month of work could be set against what the worker had been given, and the balance was computed in the employer's own book. A worker who fell sick, or whose wage was withheld, or who simply wished to leave was met with a balance that had grown while he was ill and a claim that the debt must be worked off. To prevent this, several colonial governments required the debt to be settled in money before a worker could leave, fined employers who kept workers in debt beyond a limit, or simply prohibited the advance itself; the effectiveness of each remedy depended on whether the workers could complain to anyone who was not the employer.

questions.explanation: The advance became an endless balance whenever earnings were withheld or work was interrupted, so reform had to attack the employer's book and the employer's immunity from complaint. A ban on advances alone leaves enforcement.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a law fixing a term of service changed a state
questions.stem: Explain how a law that set a long and fixed term of military service changed the state that enacted it, and why its effects were not limited to the army.

answer.exemplar: When a state replaced recruitment by long enlistment and purchase with conscription and a term fixed by law, it acquired, for the first time, a body of men it could count on and could plan with, because the number of men in arms no longer depended on the willingness of the market to sell its services. The term had to be long, since a soldier had to be trained before he was of any use, and that long term produced the two effects the government was watching for: a smaller and cheaper army in time of peace, because the mass of trained men sat in the reserve, and a settled flow of conscripts each year who were withdrawn from the villages at a predictable moment. The consequences reached far beyond the barracks, since a fixed yearly levy took the same proportion of the young men from each district and produced a generation in which a large part of the men had spent their early twenties in uniform.

questions.explanation: A fixed term gave the state a countable army and a predictable yearly levy, with the reserve keeping the peace-time force small, and the levy reached into village life. Calling it merely recruiting misses the fiscal and social reach.
questions.hint: Ask what a reserve did to the peace-time budget.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a trading concession actually conceded
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a concession over a quarter of a city conceded

stimulus.body: It is proclaimed that the ground described in the schedule is placed at the disposal of the foreign merchants, who shall govern it as a quarter of the city and shall be answerable for the order within it; and it is declared that the Chinese authorities shall not exercise any function within the ground described. The proclamation further provides that the arrangement shall be reviewed after a term of years.

questions.stem: According to the proclamation, what has been conceded?

options.text: The right to trade in a designated quarter, with the Chinese authorities still responsible for order
options.misconception: contradicts the exclusion of Chinese authority

options.text: The right to trade, the government of the quarter and the exclusion of the host authorities from it
A temporary exemption from duties, granted for a term of years pending a review
options.misconception: reduces the grant to a fiscal concession

options.text: The right to buy the ground outright, with sovereignty remaining with the central government
options.misconception: invents an outright purchase

questions.explanation: The proclamation gives the merchants the government of the ground and excludes the host authorities, so the concession was an enclave of jurisdiction as well as trade. The alternatives keep Chinese responsibility or reduce the grant to a duty exemption.
questions.hint: Ask who is excluded from the ground.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A district ordered to plant for the market
questions.learningObjective: Assess the result of ordering production for an export market

stimulus.body: The report notes that the district's area under cotton has risen year by year under the pressure of the buyers, while the area under grain has fallen by an equal amount, and that the villagers have sold their own bread to buy imported flour. The writer observes that the district is now a large producer of raw material and a small producer of food.

questions.stem: Given the report, what has the ordering of production produced?

options.text: A district that exports raw material while importing the food its own people used to grow
A district that is richer than before, since the cash crop replaced subsistence at a profit
options.misconception: reads the cash crop as a general prosperity

options.text: A district that has become self-sufficient, since the buyers built the roads and the mills
options.misconception: invents infrastructure gains as self-sufficiency

options.text: A district whose villagers chose the crop, because grain prices had fallen in the world market
options.misconception: assumes the farmers chose the crop

questions.explanation: The report describes a district that grows raw material for export and buys back the food it formerly produced. The alternatives read the change as wealth, self-sufficiency or free choice by farmers.
questions.hint: Ask what the district now imports.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A debt that could not be walked away from
questions.learningObjective: Compare debt bondage on a plantation with village debt
questions.stem: A course compares debt bondage on a plantation with the debts that tied peasants to a merchant's advance in a village. Compare what each arrangement did to the worker's freedom.

options.text: Both removed the worker's ability to choose, though one was enforced by a criminal law and the other by a running account
The plantation system freed the worker after a fixed term, while the village debt could never be settled
options.misconception: assumes terms were always honoured

options.text: The village debt was a matter of family reputation, so the peasant could always leave at a cost
options.misconception: assumes the village debt was easily avoided

options.text: Only the plantation system bound workers, since village advances were a normal form of credit
options.misconception: treats village credit as ordinary lending

questions.explanation: In both cases the worker's choice was removed, once by criminal law and once by an account that grew while the worker could not escape it. The alternatives assume honoured terms, easy exit or ordinary village credit.
questions.hint: Ask what each system removed from the worker.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Title made by a survey rather than by occupation
questions.learningObjective: Identify the chief purpose of surveying land before sale
questions.stem: A note on a land scheme in a referral letter explains that the survey is carried out before the lands are sold, and that the settled parcels are advertised in advance so that buyers can be allotted land in a fixed order. What is the chief purpose of the arrangement?

options.text: To make the land cheap, so that the settlement would proceed quickly into the interior
options.misconception: makes the scheme's purpose financial

options.text: To ensure that land is not already claimed when it is taken up, so that no two buyers receive the same ground
To collect a full census of the settlers at the same time as the land is allotted
options.misconception: confuses the survey with an enumeration

options.text: To reserve the best sections for the government, which could sell them at a later date
options.misconception: invents a reserve of prime sections

questions.explanation: Surveying first and allotting in a fixed order meant a parcel sold was already measured and not in someone else's hands, which is the point of a rectangular system. The alternatives claim cheapness, an enumeration or a reserved section.
questions.hint: Ask what the ordering of the sales prevented.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a settlement after a rebellion organised
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a restoration settlement organised and postponed
questions.stem: Explain what a restoration settlement organised after a civil war, and which questions it postponed rather than settled.

answer.exemplar: A settlement made on the return of the old rulers generally fixed what those rulers needed and quietly declined to reopen what they could not agree about. It would restore the church and the offices, confirm the property arrangements that had existed before the war, and settle the terms on which the defeated were readmitted, all in the interest of the party that had caused the disturbance. At the same time it left the questions most likely to divide the governing class unsettled: the order of succession, the command of the armed forces, and the standing of the religious minorities were each arranged in a way that granted everyone something and resolved nothing. The settlement's durability came from that ambiguity rather than from the clarity of its provisions.

questions.explanation: A restoration settlement confirmed the old rulers' interests, readmitted the defeated and deliberately left succession, the army and the sects open, so its durability came from ambiguity. The account that it settled everything misses how little it decided.
questions.hint: Ask which questions were left open.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A reform dated by the crisis that produced it
questions.learningObjective: Identify the crisis named in the preamble of a reform

stimulus.body: The Act is made in answer to the petitions which have been laid before the Parliament from many populous towns of the kingdom, and to the report of the commissioners appointed to inquire into the employment of children in the mills of the northern counties. It enacts that no person shall employ a child under a certain age in a mill or factory except upon the conditions named in this Act, and it appoints inspectors to visit the mills and to report.

questions.stem: According to the preamble, what crisis does the Act answer?

options.text: A failure of the mills to find sufficient hands, which the commissioners were to remedy
options.misconception: inverts the crisis into a labour shortage

options.text: The agitation that followed an official inquiry, which brought the conditions in the mills to public notice
A war abroad, during which the price of cotton rose and the mills could not compete
options.misconception: invents a war as the cause

options.text: A dispute between the northern manufacturers and the southern ports over the price of goods
options.misconception: invents a commercial dispute

questions.explanation: The preamble names the petitions and the commission's report as the occasion of the Act, so it answers a public agitation produced by an official inquiry. The alternatives reverse the crisis or invent a war or a commercial dispute.
questions.hint: Ask what the preamble lists first.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The shortage that a change in legal status created
questions.learningObjective: Identify the shortage caused by exempting native labourers

stimulus.body: The commission notes that since the law which exempted the subjects of the kingdom from contracts of labour abroad, the employers of the plantations have found it impossible to obtain hands from the native population, and that the labourers now employed have been brought from a neighbouring empire at great expense. The report notes that the new labourers are held under agreements of their own, and that the conditions of those agreements are fixed by the employers.

questions.stem: Given the report, what did the change in legal status create?

options.text: A shortage of native hands, met by importing workers on terms drawn up by the employers
A plentiful supply of labour, since the native population was free to choose whether to work
options.misconception: confuses legal freedom with willing supply

options.text: The end of the plantation economy, since the change removed the labour it required
options.misconception: concludes the plantations closed

options.text: A fall in wages, since employers could now hire from two labour markets at once
options.misconception: invents a wage fall from the report

questions.explanation: The exemption removed native workers from the overseas labour market, so plantations imported hands on agreements the employers drafted, a shortage met by replacing one workforce with another. The alternatives mistake freedom for willing supply or claim the plantations closed.
questions.hint: Ask why the plantations had to look abroad.

questions.topic: A bounded term of service and what it changed
questions.learningObjective: Compare a term of military service with a term of apprenticeship
questions.stem: A course compares a bounded term of military service with a bounded term of apprenticeship. Compare what each term was for.

options.text: One gave the soldier a trade to learn, while the other gave the apprentice a uniform to wear
options.misconception: swaps the purposes of the two

options.text: Both existed to shorten the working life, so that no one served beyond a certain age
options.misconception: claims both were age limits

options.text: Both existed to give the employer a cheap way to refuse responsibility for the worker
options.misconception: makes both a trick on the employer

options.text: One bound soldiers to a state that had to keep them, the other bound apprentices to a master who had to teach them

questions.explanation: A term of service fixed the reciprocal duties of soldier and state, while apprenticeship fixed those of master and apprentice. The alternatives swap the purposes or reduce both to age limits.
questions.hint: Ask which side each term bound.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a trading concession actually conceded
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a pledge of consultation conceded
questions.stem: A history entry describes an agreement by which the government of a state pledged to receive certain officials of another power, to admit their armed force, and to consult them before taking important measures. What has been conceded?

options.text: Nothing beyond the right to trade, since commercial concessions never carried political obligations
options.misconception: denies that concessions carry obligations

options.text: The right to trade on equal terms, with the pledge securing only the safety of foreign merchants
options.misconception: reduces the pledge to merchant protection

options.text: A say in the government's future decisions, and a standing right of intervention in its internal affairs
Temporary control of the armed forces, which the sovereign state would resume at the end of the term
options.misconception: makes the intervention temporary

questions.explanation: A pledge to receive foreign officials, admit their troops and consult them gives the other power a standing say in the host's decisions, which is far more than trade. The alternatives reduce it to commerce, protection or a temporary arrangement.
questions.hint: Ask what the consultation clause gave.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A district ordered to plant for the market
questions.learningObjective: Explain how market-directed planting changed a household economy
questions.stem: Explain how a district ordered to plant a crop for an outside market changed the household economy of the people who lived in it.

answer.exemplar: When a district's best land was turned over to the required crop and the household's food had to be bought instead of grown, several changes followed at once. The family lost the right to decide how its own labour would be spent, and its earnings became dependent on a price set in another market, so a bad year abroad became a hungry year at home. Credit against the future crop pulled the household into the hands of the buyers and their agents, and the land itself became the security for the advance. At the same time the district grew richer in cash and poorer in food, and the village became a place that produced a commodity for someone else.

questions.explanation: The household lost choice over labour and land, became exposed to a price set abroad, and often mortgaged its land to the buyer of the crop. The account that the scheme simply enriched the district misses these losses.
questions.hint: Ask what the household gave up to get cash.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A debt that could not be walked away from
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a clause did to a worker's choice to leave

stimulus.body: It is agreed that the said labourer shall be provided with food, clothing and lodging, the cost of which shall be advanced to him against his wages; and that the employer shall not discharge him until such advances shall have been fully repaid, and then only at a place appointed by the employer.

questions.stem: According to the clause, what does the arrangement make of the worker's choice to leave?

options.text: It removes the choice, since discharge requires repayment the worker cannot make without an employer's consent
It delays the choice by a fixed number of years, after which the worker is free to go
options.misconception: invents a fixed term not in the clause

options.text: It leaves the choice intact, since the worker may repay the advance from his wages and depart
options.misconception: ignores the employer's consent requirement

options.text: It transfers the choice to the state, which appoints the place of discharge and approves it
options.misconception: invents a role for the state

questions.explanation: Discharge required money the worker could only earn from the employer refusing to pay him out, so the choice to leave was not real. The alternatives invent a fixed term, an easy exit or a role for the state.
questions.hint: Ask who had to approve the place of departure.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Title made by a survey rather than by occupation
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a certificate system made possible

stimulus.body: The deputy surveyor records that a great part of the country has been taken up by people who never entered it, holding certificates of purchase and the right to sell them, and that the certificates pass from hand to hand at prices far above the government price. He notes that the men who actually work the land buy from these certificate holders at whatever price is asked.

questions.stem: Given the note, what does the surveying arrangement make possible?

options.text: That land can be held and traded on paper before anyone has occupied or seen it
That the survey itself becomes a commodity, since the certificate carries the right to buy
options.misconception: confuses the certificate with the survey

options.text: That the government loses the power to fix the price of land in the frontier districts
options.misconception: assumes the government set prices the note describes

options.text: That the men who work the land must wait for the certificates to be exhausted before settling
options.misconception: invents a rule about who may settle

questions.explanation: Because a certificate referred to a surveyed parcel, it could be bought and sold before anyone walked on the ground, and the worker paid the holder's price. The alternatives confuse certificate with survey or invent a price rule.
questions.hint: Ask what a buyer acquired before visiting.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a settlement after a rebellion organised
questions.learningObjective: Compare two kinds of settlement after a rebellion
questions.stem: A seminar asks what settlements after a rebellion are for, comparing a settlement that reorganised the state with one that simply restored the old order.

options.text: Both aimed at durability, but one built new institutions to achieve it and the other restored what had existed
The first aimed to punish the defeated, while the second aimed to forget the quarrel entirely
options.misconception: reduces the first settlement to punishment

options.text: The first was a compromise between victors and vanquished, while the second was a surrender by the victors
options.misconception: calls the restoration a surrender

options.text: Neither was about duration, since both were written to be revised as soon as possible
options.misconception: denies the concern with lasting order

questions.explanation: Settlements after a rising aim at durability, differing in whether it is sought through new institutions or by restoring the old ones. The alternatives reduce them to punishment, surrender or temporary measures.
questions.hint: Ask what each settlement was trying to last.
